title: Press on (Philippians 3:12–21)
hook: forgetting what lies behind, straining forward

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul moved his whole résumé into the loss column, and your line was all else is loss. Which pride did you move out of the center? Day six hundred sixty-four.

Watch the last fifty meters of a race. Nobody in the lead looks back. Coaches drill it: the moment you turn your head to see who's behind you, you lose a step. The runners lean forward, chest out, reaching for a line on the ground. Paul reaches for the same picture: a track, a line, a prize. Paul has just told the Philippians that everything behind him is loss. Now he turns around, so to speak, and faces the other way. He reaches for the language of the stadium to say what his life looks like now.

He starts with an admission. Paul, the great apostle, says he hasn't arrived. In the King James Bible: "Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended." Not yet. I haven't got hold of it. Then the famous lines: "this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus." Every phrase is a runner. Forgetting what's behind. Reaching forth, the body leaning out. The mark, the goal at the end of the track. The prize. And the verb for press is worth a second look. In Greek it's a word for chasing, pursuing hard. A few verses earlier, Paul used the very same word about his past: he had been zealous, he said, persecuting the church. Persecuting, chasing. The same energy that once hunted Christians now runs toward Christ. Paul doesn't become a calmer man. He points the same drive in a new direction. What does he mean by forgetting? Not amnesia. He remembers his past well enough to write it down a few verses earlier. He means it no longer steers. Not his old credentials, not his old wrongs. Then he widens the picture, back to the citizen word from a few days ago: "For our conversation is in heaven." You live here, he says, but your city is somewhere else. So you run.
screen: then, large: `I PRESS TOWARD THE MARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step forward. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you keep replaying, a failure, an old win, a conversation you can't stop rewriting. Notice how much of your attention it still takes. Now gently turn your head the other way. What is one small thing in front of you, today or this week, that you've been putting off while you looked back? A call. A page. An apology. A first lap. Picture yourself taking the first step toward it, just one. If you pray, you can ask for help to run. The bell holds the time.
Press on. Paul's runner's word: chase hard toward the goal, the same verb he once used for persecuting, now aimed forward.

Your line: forgetting what's behind, reaching forth. Today, do the first lap of the thing you've been postponing, even ten minutes of it, without looking back to grade the last attempt. Day six hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Philippians 3:13–14 at new beginnings, such as a new year, a graduation or a recovery.

myth: Paul says he has already reached perfection
he says plainly he hasn't got hold of it yet. that's why he keeps running.
forgetting what's behind means Paul erased his past

Paul uses the same Greek verb for pressing on that he used for persecuting the church
in 3:6 he was persecuting the church; in 3:14 he presses toward the mark.

fork.setup: you're running the last stretch of a race and you hear footsteps behind you. what do you do?
options: look back to see who it is.
forget what's behind and reach for the line.
slow down and let them pass.
fork.reveal: Paul's picture: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before."

original.note: Greek: to chase, pursue, press on. Paul uses the same verb for persecuting the church in Philippians 3:6.

trapdoor: what you thought: a motivational poster line.
what it means: Paul admits he hasn't arrived, lets the past stop steering, and runs toward the prize of God's calling.
what a scholar hears: diōkō, the verb Paul used for persecuting the church, now used for pressing on, and citizenship in heaven (3:20), picking up the citizen word of 1:27.

notes: Philippians 3:12 opens with a similar admission (not as though I had already attained); the quoted line is 3:13. Confirm.
διώκω in 3:6 (διώκων τὴν ἐκκλησίαν), 3:12 and 3:14: confirm.
πολίτευμα (3:20) as citizenship/commonwealth; KJV 'conversation' in its older sense of manner of life. Confirm gloss.
Philippi as a Roman colony: Acts 16:12. Athletic imagery is a standard reading of 3:13–14.
